extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (Math 216) / readers learning foundations of algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and precise criteria for computing scheme-theoretic images (affine-locally and when pathologies are absent), definitions and tests for locally principal closed subschemes, effective Cartier divisors, regular sequences and regular embeddings, complete intersections, and basic facts about fibered products and representable functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local computation of the scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: On an affine open Spec B of Y, define I(B) := ker( B → Γ(Spec B, π_*(O_X)) ). The scheme-theoretic image can be described locally on affines by the functions that pull back to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question addressed: given a function r/ g^n on D(g) that pulls back to zero on π^{-1}(D(g)), is there an m with r g^m = 0 when pulled back to π^{-1}(Spec B)? Three cases where the answer is yes: (i) if π^{-1}(Spec B) is reduced then take m = 1; (ii) if π^{-1}(Spec B) is affine, work with A = Γ(π^{-1}(Spec B), O_X) and find m so that r'(g')^m = 0 in A (equivalently D(g')-vanishing); (ii)' if π^{-1}(Spec B) is quasicompact cover by finitely many affines, choose m = max(m_i). Under these hypotheses one can glue and define the scheme-theoretic image as a closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: When affine-local computation is valid (Theorem 8.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is reduced or π is quasicompact, then the scheme-theoretic image of π may be computed affine-locally: on Spec A ⊂ Y it is cut out by the functions that pull back to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise hypothesis guaranteeing no pathology like Example 4; see Exercise 8.1.H for formal glueing to get a global closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between set-theoretic image and scheme-theoretic image (Corollary 8.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 8.3.4, the closure of the set-theoretic image of π is the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: the set-theoretic image is contained in the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image; the latter is closed, so closure of set-theoretic image is contained in it. Conversely, on the complement of the closure the inverse image is empty, and by local computability the scheme-theoretic image is empty there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathology example caution (Example 4 / Caution 8.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the above hypotheses pathologies can occur: there exist morphisms whose scheme-theoretic image is all of Y while the set-theoretic image is a single closed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: X = Spec k[ε_n]/((ε_n)_n) mapping to Y = Spec k[x] so pullback forces every Taylor coefficient to vanish, giving scheme-theoretic image V(0)=Y but set-theoretic image = origin; indicates hypotheses in Theorem 8.3.4 are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced reduced subscheme structure on a closed subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a closed subset X_set ⊂ Y, there is a canonical reduced closed subscheme X whose defining ideal on an affine Spec B is the radical ideal I(X_set), i.e., X|Spec B = Spec(B / I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent descriptions: (1) cut out by functions vanishing at all points of X_set; (2) scheme-theoretic image of the disjoint union of residue fields of points of X_set under the canonical maps; (3) the smallest closed subscheme whose underlying set contains X_set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction (Y_red) of a scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduction Y_red of Y is the closed subscheme obtained by shearing off nilpotents: on Spec B it corresponds to quotient by the nilradical N(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: nilradical localizes correctly (N(B)_f = N(B_f)) so this defines a closed subscheme. Informally 'shearing off the fuzz'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: global sections of the reduction need not be quotient by nilpotents (Caution 8.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not always true that Γ(U, O_{Y_red}) = Γ(U, O_Y) modulo its nilpotents for every open U ⊂ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Y = Spec k[x]/(x^n) — the function x is not nilpotent globally but is 0 on Y_red because it is locally nilpotent; this behavior is related to the pathologies like Example 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally principal closed subscheme (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme is locally principal if on a suitable open cover it is cut out by a single equation (i.e., the ideal sheaf is locally principal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can refine the cover to affine opens so that on each affine Spec A the closed subscheme is V(s) for some s ∈ Γ(Spec A, O_Y). Warning: local principality is not an obviously affine-local condition (see Exercise 5.4.N and projective hypersurface example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Cartier divisor (definition and test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme X ⊂ Y is an effective Cartier divisor if its ideal sheaf is locally generated by a single non-zerodivisor: there is an affine cover Spec A_i with X|Spec A_i = V(t_i) where each t_i ∈ A_i is a non-zerodivisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: this condition can be verified on an affine cover but not on an arbitrary affine cover; in a locally Noetherian scheme X is an effective Cartier divisor iff V(t) does not vanish on any associated point of X (Exercise 8.4.B). If D = V(t) = V(t') are two presentations on an affine Spec A with t,t' non-zerodivisors then t = u t' for a unit u ∈ A (Exercise 8.4.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular sequence (definition and basic properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an A-module M, a sequence x_1,...,x_r is an M-regular sequence if for each i the element x_i is not a zerodivisor on M/(x_1,...,x_{i-1})M (interpret i=1 as x_1 is not a zerodivisor on M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: M-regularity is preserved under localization (and more generally flat base change); certain manipulations of powers keep regularity (e.g., if x,y is regular then x^N,y is regular); order can matter in nonlocal situations (example shows x,(x−1)y regular but (x−1)y,x not); in Noetherian local rings with M finitely generated any reordering of an M-regular sequence in the maximal ideal remains regular (Theorem 8.4.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular embedding (definition and openness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A locally closed embedding π: X → Y is a regular embedding of codimension r at p ∈ X if in the local ring O_{Y,p} the ideal of X is generated by a regular sequence of length r. π is a regular embedding of codimension r if this holds at all p ∈ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The condition 'being a regular embedding at p' is open in X (Exercise 8.4.G): if it holds at p it holds in a neighborhood. Hence for quasicompact X it suffices to check at closed points. Relation: regular embedding of codimension 1 is equivalent to effective Cartier divisor under Noetherian-like hypotheses (Exercise 8.4.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Codimension r complete intersection (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme X ⊂ Y is a codimension r complete intersection if it can be written as the scheme-theoretic intersection of r effective Cartier divisors D_1,...,D_r such that at every p ∈ X the corresponding equations form a regular sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'complete intersection' means 'codimension r complete intersection for some r'. This ties algebraic (regular sequence) and geometric (effective Cartier divisors) notions together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and properties of fibered products of schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fibered products X ×_Z Y exist in the category of schemes for morphisms α: X → Z and β: Y → Z. Construction proceeds by gluing affine fibered products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings and useful facts: (i) products of schemes are not necessarily products on underlying sets (extra points can appear); (ii) however, W-valued points behave via the universal property Hom(W, X ×_Z Y) = Hom(W,X) ×_{Hom(W,Z)} Hom(W,Y); (iii) for finite type k-schemes over an algebraically closed field k, closed points of the product correspond to products of closed points (Nullstellensatz); (iv) fibered product of Noetherian schemes need not be Noetherian (counterexamples supplied). The proof strategy: handle affine case (tensor product of rings), open embeddings, then glue generally using affine covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functors must be Zariski sheaves (necessary condition for representability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a functor F: Sch^{op} → Sets is representable by a scheme X (i.e., F ≅ h_X with h_X(T) = Hom(T,X)), then F is a Zariski sheaf: morphisms to X glue over open covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: if a functor fails to satisfy the sheaf (glueing) condition it cannot be representable. Fibered products of functors always exist (pointwise), but representability of the fibered product corresponds to existence of the scheme-theoretic fibered product. Exercises develop the notion of open subfunctors and coverings in this functor-of-points language; to check openness of a subfunctor it suffices to check pullbacks along maps from representable functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open subfunctors and glueing representability
rubrics_metrics.description: A map of functors h' → h expresses h' as an open subfunctor of h if for every map h_X → h (with X a scheme), the fiber product h_X ×_h h' is representable and corresponds to an open subscheme of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functorial notion extends the usual notion of open embedding of schemes. Intersections and coverings of open subfunctors behave as expected: intersections correspond to intersections of opens, and a collection of open subfunctors covers h if their pullbacks cover each representing scheme.
